finding.claim: POST /profile/avatar fetches an attacker-supplied URL server-side with axios; the only check is an https:// prefix, so the host is unrestricted. Internal HTTPS hosts are reachable, and an https:// host can redirect to http:// internal targets such as 169.254.169.254. The response is returned only as byte length, so the bug is blind but gives a reachability oracle.

trace.note: express.json() parses the request body; no auth middleware on the route
POST /profile/avatar registered without authentication or authorization
url = req.body.avatarUrl, taken directly from the client
validation: typeof url === 'string' and url.startsWith('https://'); scheme only, no host check
axios.get(url) issues the server-side request; redirects followed by default (not verified by running)
res.json({ bytes: img.data.length }) returns only the size; non-2xx throws, and the async handler has no try/catch, giving a success/error oracle

finding.guards_checked: Type check (typeof string) at server.js:11: sound. Scheme prefix check (startsWith https://) at server.js:11: restricts scheme only, not host. Not present: hostname/IP allowlist; private, loopback, or link-local address rejection; DNS-resolution check against rebinding; port restriction; maxRedirects:0 or per-hop redirect validation; response size limit; timeout. Internal HTTPS targets need a trusted certificate unless NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 is set (deployment question, not verified).

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check is server.js:11, `typeof url !== "string" || !url.startsWith("https://")`, which is a type check plus a scheme-only prefix check. There is no hostname or IP allowlist, no private/loopback/link-local rejection, no maxRedirects:0, no timeout, and no response size limit anywhere in server.js.
verdict.reason: The attacker-controlled value `req.body.avatarUrl` (server.js:10) reaches `axios.get(url, ...)` (server.js:14) on an unauthenticated route (server.js:9), and the only validation at server.js:11 restricts the scheme to https:// without any host restriction, so the SSRF is not closed. Trace lines all exist and match the description; the one nuance is that the error path at server.js:14-15 has no try/catch, so a failed fetch produces a hung or failed request rather than a clean error response, which still gives a reachability signal but is not the explicit success/error oracle the claim describes. Redirect-following is axios's default and not verified by running, and reaching internal HTTPS hosts depends on certificate trust at deployment.

finding.claim: Not an SSRF finding: the destination host is fixed to USER_SVC. Path confusion via id values such as '..' can reach other paths on the same trusted host (low severity).

trace.note: USER_SVC constant fixes the host to http://users.internal:8080
encodeURIComponent(id) encodes '/', '?', '#', and '%'; '.' and '..' pass through
axios.get on the fixed host; dot-segments can alter the path on the same host

finding.guards_checked: encodeURIComponent at server.js:19 blocks path-separator and query injection. Host is constant, so the attacker cannot choose the destination host. Residual path confusion is low severity and not SSRF.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:19 encodeURIComponent(req.params.id) blocks '/', '?', and '#', so the attacker cannot add path segments. The destination host is a constant at server.js:7 and is used unchanged at server.js:20.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (server.js:7, 18, 19, 20 match the claims), but the attacker cannot choose the destination host, so this is not SSRF; the only residual effect is a dot-segment (`..`) normalization within the same fixed host at server.js:20, which the candidate itself rates as low-severity path confusion rather than SSRF.
